en: The Jātaka:
The Fifth Book of Birth Stories, Chapter on the Half-Units (Aḍḍhavagga)
4. The Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka “Having taken up all your goods,
O brahmin, you have crossed to the further shore.”
“Return quickly and swiftly;
rescue me from this as well.
“I am one who has not been acquainted with you for long, yet you have become a long-time friend to me.”
“Lady, you are exchanging the impermanent for the permanent;
I too, lady, would exchange you for another,
and I shall go far away from here.”
“One makes one’s body like a cluster of *eḷagalā* creepers, laughing with ‘ahuhā’;
yet here there is neither dance nor song.”
The drum is well-tuned; you have beautiful hips, O lovely one—
why indeed do you laugh at a time when there is no festival?”
“O jackal, you are a fool, dull-witted,
and lacking in wisdom;
you have lost both the fish and the carrion.”
"You meditate like one who is miserable.
"The fault of others is easy to see,
but one's own is difficult to see."
“I think you meditate on nothing but your wife and your lover. “So it is,
O King of Beasts.”
"Just as you speak, jackal;
surely, having gone from here,
I shall become subject to the will of my husband."
“Whoever steals a clay bowl,
he may as well steal a bronze bowl;
for you have indeed committed an evil deed.”
"Will you not do so again?
Thus ends the fourth Jātaka, the Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka.
